t: Obadiah: a name and nothing else
p: The book gives no father, town, king or date. Only the name, "servant of the LORD", is given.
b: Obadyah means "servant of the LORD" and was a common name: the Bible names about a dozen men called Obadiah, among them Ahab's palace steward who hid a hundred prophets (1 Kings 18:3-4). Nothing in the book ties its prophet to any of them. A vision (chazon) is the word that opens Isaiah and Nahum too, and in prophetic books it means a message received, not only something seen. The Talmud (Bavli Sanhedrin 39b) is reported to name the prophet as Ahab's steward and to call him a convert from Edom, who therefore took a God-given message against his own people; Jerome reports that Jewish teachers of his day identified him with the steward as well. These are traditions, not evidence. Many scholars think "Obadiah" may be a name attached to an anonymous oracle.

p: Hebrew has two titles side by side, Adonay YHWH. English capital letters mark the name YHWH.
b: The Hebrew name YHWH is written "the LORD" in capitals, as in most English Bibles, because Jewish readers say Adonay ("my Lord") instead of pronouncing it. Where the text has both Adonay YHWH, the Plain English Translation writes "the Lord GOD" so the two stay distinct. The phrase is a messenger formula: a prophet speaking for a king would say "This is what the king says." Here it opens a message about Edom. Like most oracles against nations (Amos 1-2; Isaiah 13-23; Jeremiah 46-51; Ezekiel 25-32), it was probably not delivered in Edom. It was spoken or written for Judah, and Edom is addressed as "you" to make a point to Judah.
orig: כֹּה־אָמַר אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה (koh amar Adonay YHWH)

a: an envoy was sent among the nations
t: The envoy and the call to arms
p: Verse 1 is nearly the same as Jeremiah 49:14. Both say a messenger is sent to call the nations against Edom.
b: Verse 1 and Jeremiah 49:14 share almost the same words, and they begin the longest overlap between the two books (see the chapter page). The "envoy" (tsir) is a messenger sent among the nations; the verse does not say who he is, though the "report" comes from the LORD. The call "Rise up!" is plural: it summons the nations as an army. The Hebrew calls Edom "her" ("against her"), the way a city or nation is often a woman. Note the difference in voice: here "we have heard" (a group listening to the LORD), in Jeremiah "I have heard" (the prophet alone). The nations are the LORD's tools, and do not know it (compare Isaiah 10:5-7).

p: Edom was proud of its strength, so "small" is the sting. The verse is almost word for word in Jeremiah 49:15.
b: The Hebrew verb is a perfect form, netatikha, "I have made you." Prophets often speak of a coming event as already done (the "prophetic perfect"), and the Plain English Translation writes "I am making" to catch that sense. Jeremiah 49:15 has the same line, ending "despised among people" where Obadiah has "greatly despised." Edom's size is the point: it lay on a rugged plateau east of the Arabah and was proud of its strongholds (verses 3-4). "Small" is also what Amos says of Jacob in Amos 7:2, 5, where Jacob is too small to survive; here the same word is turned on Edom.

p: Edom's heights were hard to attack. "Sela" may be a rock city. Whether it is Petra is doubted.
b: The Hebrew chagve sela' means "clefts of the rock" (the same pair of words describes the cracks where doves nest in Song of Songs 2:14). Edom's land is a high, steep plateau cut with ravines, and its capital Bozrah (modern Buseirah) sat on a ridge. Sela' ("rock") is also a place name: 2 Kings 14:7 says King Amaziah took "Sela" in war and renamed it Joktheel. Because Greek petra also means "rock," Petra has often been called Sela, but Petra's great days came under the Nabataeans after Edom's fall, and the identification is debated. Excavations at Umm el-Biyara, Tawilan and Buseirah show Edomite settlement in the 700s to 500s BC. Jeremiah 49:16 has the same Hebrew for "clefts of the rock," "the pride of your heart" (zedon libbekha) and "I will bring you down," and the Plain English Translation renders them the same way in both books. Jeremiah adds "the terror you cause" (tiflatzteka) and ends "who hold the height of the hill," where Obadiah says "whose home is the height."
r: Jeremiah 49:16; 2 Kings 14:7; Isaiah 16:1; Song of Songs 2:14

a: Who will lower me to the ground?
p: The same boast is put in the mouth of Babylon's king in Isaiah 14. Pride that says "who can touch me?" is a frequent target.
b: Edom's boast, "Who will lower me to the ground?", has no match in Jeremiah 49:16, which has the cliff, the nest and the fall but no boast. It does echo other proud speeches: the king of Babylon who says he will go up to heaven and is brought down to Sheol (Isaiah 14:13-15), the builders of Babel who want a tower into the sky (Genesis 11:4), and the prince of Tyre who says he is a god (Ezekiel 28:2-9). The Hebrew verb in "lower" is the same one used in verse 4, "I will bring you down." The LORD answers the boast in his own words. Amos 9:2-3 makes the same point from the other side: no height or hiding place is out of the LORD's reach. "Ground" (erets) can also mean the underworld.

p: The eagle nests on high crags. The stars here picture a height no human reaches.
b: The Hebrew nesher is usually translated "eagle," but it can also be the griffon vulture, which nests on high cliff ledges. In either case the picture is a bird's nest too high to reach. "Among the stars" takes the picture beyond any mountain, as in Isaiah 14:13, where the proud king wants a throne "higher than the stars of God," and Job 20:6. The point of the sentence is the second half, "from there I will bring you down." Jeremiah 49:16 has the eagle line but not the stars. Edom's cities were built into mountain rock, so any reader who knew them would feel how high the claim was.

p: Jeremiah 49:9 puts the grape harvesters first. Obadiah puts the thieves first, and adds a cry.
b: The two oracles share this picture but order it differently. In Jeremiah 49:9 the grape harvesters come first and the night thieves second. In Obadiah the thieves come first (named twice: "thieves," "robbers in the night"), then the harvesters. The cry "how ruined you are!" (eikh nidmeita) has no match in Jeremiah. The argument is from the lesser to the greater: even thieves take only what they need, and even a harvest leaves gleanings, but Edom will be searched through completely (verse 6). Jeremiah 49:10 says the LORD himself has stripped Esau bare; Obadiah says it more quietly, with a passive verb.

t: Gleanings: what the law left for the poor
p: Israel's law told harvesters to leave some grapes. Edom's looters will leave none.
b: Gleanings ('olelot) are the grapes left on the vine after the main picking. The law told Israelite farmers not to strip the vineyard a second time, but to leave the leftovers for the poor and the foreigner (Leviticus 19:10; Deuteronomy 24:21). Isaiah uses the picture for the few left after a judgment (Isaiah 24:13). Here the question shows how complete the coming ruin is: ordinary harvesters follow the rule and leave a few grapes, but the enemies of Edom will not.

p: Esau, Jacob's twin, is the founder of Edom. Obadiah uses the name seven times, "Edom" only twice.
b: Esau was Jacob's twin. His red hair and his meal of red stew gave him the name Edom ("red"), and he settled in Seir (Genesis 25:25-30; 36:1, 8). Obadiah uses "Esau" seven times (verses 6, 8, 9, 18 twice, 19, 21) and "Edom" only twice (verses 1, 8). Using the ancestor's name keeps the family story in view: this is the old quarrel between brothers (verse 10). The phrase "Mount Esau" (verses 8, 9, 19, 21) points to Edom's hill country, Mount Seir. The Plain English Translation says "Esau" where the Hebrew does.
r: Genesis 25:25-30; Genesis 36:1; Genesis 36:8; Deuteronomy 2:4-5; Jeremiah 49:8; Jeremiah 49:10

p: Edom's secret treasure is dug out. Jeremiah 49:10 says "secret places."
b: Matspunav comes from tsafan, "to hide, store up." It means things hidden away: stores of goods, treasures, or even secret places. Jeremiah 49:10 uses a different word, mistarav, "his hiding places." The verb nivu ("pried out") is rare, and its sense is guessed from context; the Greek renders it with a general word for seizing, and both scrolls (4QXIIg and Mur 88) have the same consonants as the Leningrad Codex. The picture is a house-to-house search that leaves nothing unturned, the opposite of the thieves in verse 5.

p: The verse names allies who turned on Edom. No event is named, and scholars guess several.
b: "Men of your covenant" are allies bound by treaty; "men of your peace" are friends who greeted Edom with "peace." The verse does not say who they are. Views: (1) Edom's neighbors, such as Moab and Ammon, whose envoys joined Edom's at Zedekiah's court (Jeremiah 27:3); (2) the Babylonians, whom Edom may have served; (3) the Arab tribes and the Nabataeans, who pushed into Edom in the 500s to 300s BC (Malachi 1:2-5 says Edom's hills had been laid waste); (4) a later, unnamed event. "Sent you away to the border" can mean driven out of the land, or seen off with fair words to the frontier and then abandoned. The Plain English Translation keeps both readings open.

t: A rare word: trap, wound or ambush?
p: The Hebrew mazor is uncertain. The Greek says "ambush."
b: Mazor elsewhere seems to mean a wound or a bandage (Hosea 5:13; Jeremiah 30:13). That would give "they set a wound beneath you," which makes poor sense. The Greek translators wrote "ambush" and most modern translators write "trap" or "snare," as the Plain English Translation does. A further problem: the Hebrew is literally "your bread they set a trap under you." The Plain English Translation reads it as "those who eat your bread," that is, guests and friends at table (compare Psalm 41:9). The Greek has no word for "your bread" at all; see the variant. The scrolls 4QXIIg and Mur 88 both have "your bread."
orig: לַחְמְךָ יָשִׂימוּ מָזוֹר תַּחְתֶּיךָ (lachmekha yasimu mazor tachtekha)

p: The line switches to third person. It sets up the word "understanding" in verse 8.
b: The speech has been to "you" all through. Here it turns to "he," as if the speaker turned away from Edom to tell others. A similar shift happens in Jeremiah 49:10 ("he cannot hide"). The word is tevunah, "understanding," and it is the key to the next verse. Edom had a name for wisdom (see verse 8). The verse says the wise nation does not see what its friends are doing to it. Some translators read it as "there is no understanding in it," that is, no one sees the trap. The Plain English Translation keeps the plain Hebrew.

p: Edom, and especially Teman, had a name for wisdom. Job's friend Eliphaz came from Teman.
b: Jeremiah 49:7 asks, "Is wisdom finished in Teman?" Teman was a place or clan in Edom's south (verse 9), and one of the three friends who visit Job is Eliphaz the Temanite (Job 2:11). Job himself lives in Uz, which Lamentations 4:21 places in Edom's territory, and Genesis 36:28 names an Uz among Seir's clans. So Edom was thought of as a home of wisdom teaching, such as the book of Job. Obadiah's words are meant to hurt for that reason: the nation that prided itself on counsel will lose it. Compare Isaiah 19:11-13, where Egypt's wise men lose their counsel in the same way.

t: "That day": the first of the days
p: The word "day" runs through the book and ends in "the day of the LORD" (verse 15).
b: "On that day" looks ahead to the LORD's action. After this, "day" returns ten times in verses 11-14, always for the day Jerusalem fell, and then in verse 15 as "the day of the LORD." The book is built on the word. The question form ("Will I not...?") expects the answer "Yes, I will." The speaker is the LORD ("the LORD declares," ne'um YHWH), not the prophet.

p: Teman is a place or clan in Edom's south. The prophets pair it with Bozrah.
b: Teman means "south" and also names a grandson of Esau (Genesis 36:11, 15). As a place, Teman stood in Edom, though where is debated: the south of the country, or a town such as Tawilan. Amos 1:12 and Jeremiah 49:20-22 pair Teman with Bozrah, as the two ends of Edom. Ezekiel 25:13 says "from Teman to Dedan." Habakkuk 3:3 has God coming "from Teman," a reminder that old Israelite memory placed the LORD's home in the south (compare Judges 5:4). Calling Teman's warriors "shattered" follows the loss of its wise.

t: Brother Jacob: the old family quarrel
p: "Brother" matters here: Edom and Israel were kin, and the law said so.
b: Jacob and Esau were twins who fought before they were born (Genesis 25:22-26), and Esau vowed to kill Jacob (Genesis 27:41). They made peace (Genesis 33), but the quarrel returned in their descendants. When Israel asked passage through Edom, the Edomites refused, though Moses had called Edom "your brother" (Numbers 20:14-21). Deuteronomy 23:7 tells Israel not to hate an Edomite, "for he is your brother." Obadiah's charge rests on this kinship: Edom did not just do harm, it betrayed its own family. Amos 1:11 says Edom "chased down his brother with the sword" and kept his fury. "Jacob" here means the nation, especially Judah (see verse 12).
r: Genesis 25:22-26; Genesis 27:41; Numbers 20:14-21; Deuteronomy 23:7; Amos 1:11; Psalm 137:7; Lamentations 4:21-22; Malachi 1:2-3

a: You stood aside on that day
p: The usual answer is the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC. An older answer points to the 800s BC.
b: Obadiah does not name the day. The commonest view is 586 BC, when Babylon took Jerusalem (2 Kings 25). Psalm 137:7 asks the LORD to remember what the people of Edom did on the day of Jerusalem; Lamentations 4:21-22 says Edom will be punished; Ezekiel 25:12-14 and 35:5-15 charge Edom with the same crime. Foreigners entering the gates and casting lots for the city fit a conquest of the whole city, and the strong echoes with Jeremiah and Ezekiel point to the 500s. An older view dates the book to the reign of Jehoram, when Edom revolted (2 Kings 8:20-22) and raiders carried off the palace's goods (2 Chronicles 21:16-17); a third event is the Edomite raid under Ahaz (2 Chronicles 28:17). The Hebrew for "stood aside" suits an onlooker, not a fighter (compare Psalm 38:11).
r: 2 Kings 25:8-11; Psalm 137:7; Lamentations 4:21-22; Ezekiel 25:12-14; Ezekiel 35:5-15; 2 Kings 8:20-22; 2 Chronicles 21:16-17; 2 Chronicles 28:17; Psalm 38:11

p: The Hebrew chayil can mean wealth, an army or strength. The Greek says "force."
b: Chayil is a wide word: strength, a fighting force, an army, or wealth. The Greek renders it with "force" in verses 11 and 13. The Plain English Translation reads "wealth" because the same word is the object of looting in verse 13, and because "carried off" (a verb used for taking captives) fits both people and goods. Either way, the sense is that the invaders took what mattered most, and Edom did nothing. If "army" is meant, Judah's forces were taken captive; in 2 Kings 24:14-16 the army and craftsmen are among those deported.

p: Conquerors divided captives and plunder by lot. Joel and Nahum use the same picture.
b: Casting lots was how conquerors shared captives and goods. Joel 3:3 charges the nations with casting lots for "my people" and trading boys for prostitutes; Nahum 3:10 says the nobles of Thebes were given out by lot. Here the lot is cast "for Jerusalem," as if the city itself were spoil. Obadiah, Joel 3:3 and Nahum 3:10 all use the same pair of words, yadad (cast) and goral (lot), which suggests a stock phrase for dividing captives. Jonah 1:7 uses a different verb (nafal, in the hiphil) for the sailors' lot, so it is a different matter. The Plain English Translation keeps "cast lots" and does not say how the lot was cast.

a: You were just like one of them
p: Edom is not accused of fighting, but of standing with the invaders as one of them.
b: The charge is carefully worded. Edom "stood aside" (verse 11), "looked on with delight" (verses 12-13), took part in the loot (verse 13) and blocked the escape routes (verse 14). Psalm 137:7 records the Edomites calling for the city to be torn bare to its foundation. Ezekiel 35:5 says Edom handed Israel over to the sword. How far Edom took part in the fighting is unknown: the text says "like one of them," not "with them." Nothing outside the Bible gives a detailed record of Edom's part in 586 BC.

a: Do not look on with delight
t: Eight "do nots": a command or a regret?
p: The Hebrew uses a form that can mean "do not" or, looking back, "you should not have."
b: Verses 12-14 have eight lines that begin with the Hebrew 'al plus an imperfect verb, the usual way to say "do not." Some forms are true jussives (14b tasger); 13c tishlachnah carries an added ending. Many scholars read them as warnings spoken as if the prophet stood in the scene on the day; others read them as a rebuke of what Edom had already done, "you should not have." The form itself allows both. The Greek translators read them as ordinary commands. Verse 11 and verse 15 both look back at what Edom did, so the "you should not have" reading is slightly the more natural to this note. The commands read well too, and the Plain English Translation does not choose: it keeps the plain commands and lets the reader hear either. "Look on with delight" is a Hebrew idiom for gloating (Psalm 54:7; Micah 7:10; Ezekiel 35:15). Proverbs 24:17-18 gives the same lesson as a rule: do not rejoice when your enemy falls.

p: Verse 12 is the only place the book names Judah. Elsewhere it says Jacob, Zion or Jerusalem.
b: "Jacob" (verse 10), "Judah" (verse 12), "my people" (verse 13) and "Jerusalem" (verse 11) all mean the same people. Naming Judah in particular ties the book to the southern kingdom, whose capital fell in 586 BC. Verse 18 names Joseph, the northern tribes, to widen the hope. The Hebrew "sons of Judah" is simply "the people of Judah."

p: The Hebrew is "do not make your mouth big." Ezekiel charges Edom with the same fault.
b: The idiom is "make your mouth big" (tagdel pikha), meaning to boast and speak proudly. In Ezekiel 35:13 the LORD says to Edom that they talked big against him, with the same Hebrew verb and the word "mouth." The sin is not only joy at disaster but arrogant words about it. Psalm 137:7 records what the words were. A boast spoken against God's people is heard by God as a boast against him.

p: The speaker is the LORD: Judah is "my people." The gate is where a conquered city is entered.
b: The voice of verse 13 is the LORD's, since only he can call Judah "my people." A city's gate was the place of law and business and the weak point in its defense; to enter the gate of a fallen city was to come in as a conqueror or a scavenger. The Hebrew shifts between "their" and "his" here ('eidam, "their calamity," against ra'ato and 'eido, "his calamity"); the Plain English Translation uses "their" in verses 13 and 14 so the lines read smoothly. The word 'eid, "calamity," is the one in Deuteronomy 32:35, which says the day of their calamity is near.

a: reach out a hand for their wealth
p: Edom is accused of joining the looters. Hebrew has "send" with the hand left out.
b: The Hebrew verb is shalach, "send," and the object "hand" is understood: "do not send your hand against their wealth" (compare Genesis 22:12; Exodus 24:11 for the idiom). The thing grabbed is chayil, the same word as in verse 11. Looting a city already taken fits Ezekiel 35:12-13 and the Edomites in Ezekiel 36:5 who took the land as their own. The repeated "on the day of their calamity" beats like a drum across the verse.

a: Do not stand at the crossroads
p: Fugitives from Jerusalem ran for the passes and roads. Edomites waited to catch them.
b: Perek is a rare word for a place where roads divide or cross, a fork or a mountain pass. The picture is of Edomites posted where refugees from Jerusalem had to pass, killing or capturing those who got away, and handing "those who are left" to the Babylonian army. Two Hebrew words are in play. Palit (14a, "survivors") shares its root with peletah in verse 17, so the book sets Edom cutting off Judah's "survivors" against Zion's "survivors" (verse 17). Sarid (14b, "those who are left") returns in verse 18 as "No one will be left"; Joel 2:32 uses both words. "Hand over" (sagar, "shut up, deliver up") is the verb used of surrendering a fugitive (Deuteronomy 23:15; compare Amos 1:6, 9, where Gaza and Tyre are charged with handing over whole communities to Edom). Jeremiah 40:11 shows other Judeans fleeing to Edom, Moab and Ammon and later returning, so Edom's behavior may have been mixed. The Greek reads "close in on" rather than "hand over."

a: the day of the LORD is near
t: The day of the LORD begins here
p: The book turns from Jerusalem's day to the LORD's day. Other prophets use the phrase too.
b: Verses 11-14 repeat "on the day" ten times for the day Jerusalem fell. Verse 15 answers: "the day of the LORD is near." The phrase appears in Isaiah 13:6, Ezekiel 30:3, Joel 1:15, 2:1, 3:14, Amos 5:18-20 and Zephaniah 1:7, 14. It is a day when the LORD acts to judge, and it is "near" because it is coming soon. Here it is "against all the nations," so Edom is one case of a rule. In the Hebrew order of the Twelve, Joel (with its day of the LORD) comes two books before Obadiah, and Joel 3:14 calls it a day of decision for the nations.
r: Isaiah 13:6; Ezekiel 30:3; Joel 1:15; Joel 2:1; Joel 3:14; Amos 5:18-20; Zephaniah 1:7

t: "As you did, it will be done to you"
p: This is the rule that fits the punishment to the crime. Other prophets state the same rule.
b: Obadiah's rule of repayment matches the old principle that the punishment fits the crime (Exodus 21:23-25; Judges 1:6-7, where a king who maimed others is maimed himself). Habakkuk 2:8, 16 says the same of the plunderer: those who plundered are plundered, and those who made others drink in shame will be shamed. Joel 3:4, 7 uses almost the same Hebrew for "your payback will return on your own head." "Payback" (gemul) means what is due, the ripened fruit of an act. The New Testament repeats the pattern as a principle: Matthew 7:2; Galatians 6:7; Revelation 18:6. See the card on payback.
r: Judges 1:6-7; Habakkuk 2:8; Habakkuk 2:16; Joel 3:4; Joel 3:7; Psalm 137:8; Jeremiah 50:15; Jeremiah 50:29; Matthew 7:2; Galatians 6:7; Revelation 18:6

a: You drank on my holy mountain
t: The cup: who drank, and who will
p: The verb "drank" is plural. Either Judah drank the cup of judgment, or Edom and the nations celebrated.
b: The Hebrew "you drank" is plural, so it cannot be Edom alone. Two readings: (1) Judah drank the cup of the LORD's anger on Zion, in the fall of Jerusalem, and now the nations will drink it too (Jeremiah 25:15-29; Isaiah 51:17-23, where the cup is taken from Jerusalem and handed to her tormentors; Lamentations 4:21, where it passes to Edom). (2) Edom and others drank in celebration on the temple hill, and the cup of judgment will now come to them. Both pictures use the cup of wrath (Psalm 75:8; Habakkuk 2:16). Jeremiah 49:12 has a related thought: those who were not meant to drink drank anyway, and Edom will not escape. "On and on" is tamid, "continually."
r: Jeremiah 25:15-29; Jeremiah 49:12; Isaiah 51:17-23; Lamentations 4:21; Psalm 75:8; Habakkuk 2:16

p: La'u is rare. The Greek has "go down", and some think the Hebrew means "stagger."
b: The verb la'u (from la'a) is very rare. It is usually taken as "gulp, swallow," from a root that suits drinking. Others compare a similar root meaning "to babble, stagger" and read "they will drink and stagger." The Greek has "they will drink and come down" (see the variant). The cup image is the same in each case: the nations drink until they cannot stand, then they disappear, "as if they had never been," a phrase like Job 10:19 and Psalm 37:10.

a: But on Mount Zion there will be survivors
p: The line is almost Joel 2:32. Christians and Jews have read the "survivors" and the "house of Jacob" in different ways.
b: Obadiah 17 and Joel 2:32 (3:5 in Hebrew) share "on Mount Zion ... there will be survivors," and Joel 3:17 says Jerusalem will be holy. In the Hebrew order Joel and then Amos come before Obadiah, so the Twelve link them. The "survivors" are the remnant of Judah, those who lived through 586 BC and the exile. Jewish readers have taken the promise as the return and rebuilding, and as a hope still to come. Many Christians read Zion as the church, or as the heavenly Jerusalem (Hebrews 12:22); others hold that the promise to the Jewish people still stands (Romans 11:25-29). See the card at verses 17-21.

p: Peletah means a group that escapes. Joel 2:32 has the same word.
b: Peletah is an escape, or those who escape. It names the remnant. Verse 14 uses palit, from the same root, for the survivors Edom cut off; the Plain English Translation says "survivors" in both places. Joel 2:32 uses the same word, and the Plain English Translation follows that verse's wording ("survivors"). The Greek has "salvation" (soteria). The idea of a surviving remnant runs through the prophets (Isaiah 4:2; 37:32), and Zion is the place where the remnant stands.

t: Taking possession: a word that repeats
p: The verb "take over" (yarash) returns in verses 19-20. The noun beside it comes from the same root.
b: Yarash means to take possession, to inherit, and also to dispossess. It appears in verses 17, 19 (twice) and 20, and the noun morash ("property") comes from it. The theme is a reversal: those who were driven out will take over the land again. The Plain English Translation does not try to keep the wordplay. A different pointing of the same consonants yields "those who dispossessed them," and the Greek and a scroll support that reading (see the variant). The sense would then be that Jacob takes over its former occupiers. The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic vowel marks.

a: The house of Jacob will be a fire
p: Fire and straw are old pictures for judgment. Jacob and Joseph, the south and north, are joined.
b: The picture is of a spark catching in dry stubble. Isaiah 10:17 says the light of Israel will become a fire and the Holy One a flame; Malachi 4:1 (3:19 in Hebrew) says the wicked will be "stubble" in the day of the LORD. Exodus 15:7 uses the same word (qash) for Pharaoh's army burned like straw. "Joseph" names the northern tribes (Ephraim and Manasseh, Joseph's sons), so Jacob and Joseph together stand for the whole people, south and north, reunited, as in Ezekiel 37:15-22. The Plain English Translation says "stubble," the dry stalks left in a field after harvest.

a: No one will be left of the house of Esau
p: Edomites lived on in Idumea and joined the Jewish revolt. Readers differ on what "no one left" means.
b: Edom's kingdom did end, but Edomites did not vanish. Pushed west by Arab tribes and the Nabataeans, they settled in southern Judea, called Idumea. Judas Maccabeus fought "the sons of Esau" there (1 Maccabees 5:3, 65), and John Hyrcanus forced the Idumeans to be circumcised and join the Jewish people (Josephus, Antiquities 13.9.1). Herod the Great came from an Idumean family; Obadiah says nothing about him. Idumean troops joined the Jewish revolt of AD 66-70 (Josephus, War 4.4.4-5.1). Readers differ: some say the verse is a vivid exaggeration, since Edomites lived on (Malachi 1:4 pictures Edom saying "we will rebuild" and the LORD refusing); some say the Edom of Obadiah (the kingdom) did end; others hold that "Esau" stands for all enemies of God's people, so the promise is not tied to one nation.

t: From the Negev to Gilead: the map
p: The lists name lands on all four sides of Judah. Many do not fit any conquest Obadiah's world knew.
b: South: the Negev takes Mount Esau. West: the foothills (the Shephelah) take the Philistines' land. North: Ephraim's and Samaria's countryside. East: Benjamin takes Gilead, across the Jordan. The Plain English Translation supplies "the people of" before the Negev and the Shephelah and "the land of" before the Philistines; the Hebrew has just "the Negev," "the Shephelah," "the Philistines." The Greek makes the Negev's people those living there and reads "plain of Samaria." The lists match no known historical conquest. The promise is of a restored people spreading out in every direction, a bigger map than Judah's in Obadiah's day. The lists in verse 20 go farther, to Phoenicia and perhaps Asia Minor. Amos 9:12, in the book before Obadiah in the Hebrew Twelve, speaks of taking "the remnant of Edom."

a: As for the exiles of this army of Israelites
t: The hardest verse in the book
p: The Hebrew of verse 20 is hard. Nearly every phrase is debated.
b: Three points. (1) Hachel hazeh, "this army" (or "this rampart"): the scroll Mur 88 has the same consonants as the Leningrad Codex; the Greek reads "the beginning." (2) Asher kena'anim, "who [are] Canaanites," has no verb. The Plain English Translation supplies "will take Canaan's land," following the later verb "take" in the verse; others read "who are among the Canaanites." (3) Zarephath is a Phoenician town near Sidon, where Elijah stayed with a widow (1 Kings 17:9; Luke 4:26). So the northern exiles are to take the coast as far as Zarephath, and the Jerusalem exiles the cities of the Negev. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew's two-part pattern.

p: Sepharad is named only here. Most scholars think it is Sardis in Asia Minor. Later Jews read it as Spain.
b: Sepharad (Sefarad) is named nowhere else in the Bible. The most common identification is Sardis, the capital of Lydia in western Asia Minor. The Persians called Lydia Sparda, and an Aramaic inscription from Sardis is usually cited as spelling the name with the same consonants. Other guesses are a place in Media or Syria. The Greek reads "Ephrathah"; the Latin of Jerome has "Bosphorus." The Aramaic Targum reads Sepharad as Spain. The equation of Zarephath with France is found in the Talmud (Bavli Yoma 10a) and was followed by medieval Jewish commentators. That is why Jews of the Middle Ages called Spain and France Sefarad and Tsarfat, and why Spanish and Portuguese Jews are called Sephardic. That later use is reception, not what the Hebrew meant. The Plain English Translation keeps the name.

a: Rescuers will go up on Mount Zion
p: The word is the one used for the judges who saved Israel. The Hebrew does not say who these are.
b: Moshi'im are people who save or rescue, the word used for the judges raised up to deliver Israel (Judges 3:9, 15; Nehemiah 9:27). The Plain English Translation writes "rescuers" there too. The book does not say who these are. Views: leaders of the returned community; a future deliverer or the Messiah and those who help him (medieval Jewish commentators often read the end of the book of the coming redemption); the Maccabees, who conquered Idumea (1 Maccabees 5:65; Josephus, Antiquities 13.9.1); or, in some Christian reception, the apostles or Christ himself. The Plain English Translation says "on Mount Zion" because the Hebrew has be-har; the Greek reads "from Mount Zion, to take vengeance on Mount Esau," a bigger difference (see the variant at "to judge"). Mur 88 writes the word in a shorter spelling, and the Greek reads "those who are saved" (see the variant). "To judge" can also mean "to rule" or "to give justice."

a: royal power will belong to the LORD
t: The last line: the LORD's rule
p: The last line says the whole book comes to the LORD's rule. The words echo Psalm 22:28.
b: Hamelukhah is an abstract noun, "kingship, royal power." Psalm 22:28 uses the same word: "Royal power is the LORD's; he is the ruler of the nations." The sentence ends the book with its real subject: not Edom's fall nor Judah's return, but the LORD's rule. Zechariah 14:9 says the same (the LORD will be king over all the earth), as do Daniel 7:27 and Revelation 11:15. Jesus's prayer "your kingdom come" (Matthew 6:10) is often heard against this background. Jewish tradition places this line among the kingship verses of the New Year liturgy.
